title: Slash Commands & Skills
description: Built-in commands, your own reusable commands, and skills Claude loads on demand.

theory.title: The built-in toolbox
theory.body:
Type `/` in a session to open the command menu. A few Kip uses daily:
• `/clear` starts a fresh conversation (empty context)
• `/compact` **summarizes** the conversation to free context, but keeps going
• `/init` creates a `CLAUDE.md` guide for the project
• `/model` switches models
• `/rewind` rolls back to an earlier point
• `/usage` (alias `/cost`) shows usage, and `/help` lists everything

theory.title: Write your own command
theory.body:
A custom command is just a Markdown file. The **file name** becomes the **command name**:
• `.claude/commands/fix-issue.md` → `/fix-issue` (project, commit it to share with the team)
• `~/.claude/commands/fix-issue.md` → `/fix-issue` in **every** project (personal)

To run it, type the command, a space, then any arguments. Everything after the name is passed into the file as `$ARGUMENTS`.

Commands have been merged into **skills**, but `.claude/commands/` files keep working.
theory.code:
mkdir -p .claude/commands
# write .claude/commands/fix-issue.md, then in a session:
> /fix-issue 482        # $ARGUMENTS becomes "482"

theory.title: Anatomy of a command file
theory.body:
The optional top block between two `---` lines is **YAML frontmatter**: settings written as `key: value`, one per line.
• `description:` short label shown in the `/` menu
• `argument-hint:` shows what to type after the command, e.g. `[issue-number]`
• (also allowed: `allowed-tools:` and `model:`)

Below the second `---` is the **prompt** Claude receives. `$ARGUMENTS` (dollar sign + capitals) is replaced with what you typed, so `/fix-issue 482` sends "Fix issue #482...".
theory.code:
---
description: Fix a GitHub issue by number
argument-hint: [issue-number]
---
Fix issue #$ARGUMENTS. Read the issue, find the root cause,
write a failing test, then fix it.

exercises.prompt: Match each built-in command to what it does.

pairs.right: Roll back to an earlier point

exercises.explanation: Built-in commands control the session itself, so knowing them saves you from asking Claude to do housekeeping in plain words.

exercises.prompt: You create `.claude/commands/fix-issue.md`. How do you run it?
exercises.explanation: Claude Code turns the file name (minus `.md`) into the command name, so `fix-issue.md` becomes `/fix-issue`.

exercises.prompt: Where do you put a command you want available in ALL your projects?
exercises.explanation: The `~/.claude/` folder is personal configuration in your home directory, so its commands follow you into every project.

exercises.prompt: Which body makes a better /review-diff command?
options: Review the staged diff for bugs, missing tests and security issues. Focus on $ARGUMENTS if provided. List findings by severity with file:line references.
exercises.explanation: A command is reused many times, so spelling out scope, criteria and output format once makes every run consistent.

exercises.prompt: Complete this command file so it shows a description and passes the file path through.
exercises.code:
---
___: Write unit tests for a file
argument-hint: [file-path]
---
Write thorough unit tests for $___.
Cover edge cases and run the test suite afterwards.
exercises.explanation: `description` labels the command in the `/` menu, and `$ARGUMENTS` is swapped for the typed text so one file works for any input.
exercises.hint: Frontmatter is key: value lines between --- markers; the label key is description, and $ARGUMENTS is the placeholder for what you type after the command.

steps: Add changelog.md with a description in frontmatter
Write the instructions, using $ARGUMENTS for the version
Commit the file so teammates get it too
exercises.explanation: A command is just a Markdown file in the repo, so committing it is all it takes to share it with your team.

exercises.prompt: Your context is filling up but you want to keep the same conversation going. Type the slash command that summarizes the conversation to free up space.
exercises.hint: Pattern: /<command>. Not /clear (that wipes everything); the one that compresses.
exercises.explanation: `/compact` replaces the history with a summary so you keep the thread, while `/clear` would throw it away.

exercises.prompt: Type the slash command that generates a CLAUDE.md guide for this project.
exercises.explanation: `/init` scans the project and writes a CLAUDE.md so future sessions start with the right context.

exercises.prompt: Your project has a /fix-issue command. Run it, passing issue number 482 as the argument.
exercises.explanation: Everything after the command name is substituted for `$ARGUMENTS`, which is how one command handles any issue number.

theory.title: What is a skill?
theory.body:
A **skill** is a folder containing a `SKILL.md` file. The folder name is the skill name:
• `.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` (project, shared)
• `~/.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` (personal)

Claude reads each skill's `description` and **loads the skill automatically when it is relevant**. You can also invoke it yourself with `/<name>`. Because it is a folder, a skill can bundle extra files like scripts and templates next to `SKILL.md`.
theory.code:
.claude/skills/
└── release-notes/
    ├── SKILL.md
    └── template.md      # optional extra file

theory.title: Anatomy of SKILL.md
theory.body:
Same shape as a command file: YAML frontmatter between `---` lines, then Markdown instructions.
• `name:` the skill's name (matches the folder)
• `description:` **what it does and when to use it**. Claude decides whether to load the skill from this line, so be specific.
• `disable-model-invocation: true` means only **you** can trigger it with `/deploy`, never Claude on its own. `true` and `false` are written without quotes.

Everything below the second `---` is what Claude follows when the skill runs.
theory.code:
---
name: deploy
description: Deploys the app to staging. Use when the user
  asks to deploy.
disable-model-invocation: true
---
1. Run ./scripts/deploy.sh staging
2. Report the URL it prints.

theory.title: Who gets to trigger it
theory.body:
• Default: both you (`/name`) and Claude (when the description matches) can.
• `disable-model-invocation: true`: only **you** can (great for `/deploy`).
• `user-invocable: false`: only **Claude** can.

Type `/skills` to list the skills available in this session. A file at `.claude/commands/deploy.md` and a skill at `.claude/skills/deploy/SKILL.md` both create `/deploy`; skills are recommended for new work because they support extra files.

exercises.prompt: Where does a project skill named `pdf-forms` live?
exercises.explanation: Each skill is its own folder named after the skill, which lets it hold SKILL.md plus any supporting files.

exercises.prompt: What does Claude use to decide whether to load a skill automatically?
exercises.explanation: Claude compares your task to each skill's description, so the description is what makes a skill load at the right time.

exercises.prompt: Match each skill piece to its role.

pairs.right: Tells Claude when to use it

exercises.explanation: Frontmatter fields control how a skill is discovered and who may trigger it, while the body holds the actual instructions.

exercises.prompt: Which skill description will help Claude load it at the right moment?
options: description: Generates Prisma migration files. Use when the user asks to change the database schema or add a table.
exercises.explanation: Claude matches tasks against the description, so saying what the skill does and when to use it is what triggers it.

exercises.prompt: What can a skill do that a single command file cannot?
options: Bundle supporting files like scripts and templates in its folder
exercises.explanation: Because a skill is a directory, it can carry scripts and templates alongside SKILL.md, which a single command file cannot.

exercises.prompt: Finish this SKILL.md so Claude knows when to use it, but only you can trigger it.
exercises.code:
---
name: deploy
___: Deploys the app to staging. Use when the user asks to deploy.
disable-model-invocation: ___
---
Run the deploy script and report the URL.
exercises.explanation: `description` tells Claude what the skill is for, and `disable-model-invocation: true` reserves triggering for you, which suits risky actions like deploys.
exercises.hint: Frontmatter keys are lowercase with colons: description: <what and when>; disable-model-invocation takes true or false (no quotes).

exercises.prompt: Build a project skill for writing API docs.
steps: Write SKILL.md with name and description frontmatter
Add instructions, plus any helper script in the folder
Ask for API docs, or type /api-docs
Check that Claude followed the skill's steps
exercises.explanation: A skill is just a folder with SKILL.md, so once it exists it runs either from a matching request or by its `/name`.

exercises.prompt: Inside a session, type the slash command that lists the skills available right now.
exercises.hint: Pattern: / + the plural of what you are listing.
exercises.explanation: `/skills` shows which skills are loaded, so you can confirm a new skill was picked up.

exercises.scenario: Ask Claude to create a project skill that writes commit messages following your team's Conventional Commits rules.
exercises.sample: Our team's commit messages are inconsistent. Create a project skill at @.claude/skills/commit-message/SKILL.md. Base the rules on the commit section of @CONTRIBUTING.md (Conventional Commits: type(scope): summary, max 72 chars, body explains why). Give it a description that says to use it whenever I ask for a commit message, and include two good examples. Constraints: keep it under 40 lines and don't touch any existing skills. Done when /skills lists it and you show me the file.
exercises.explanation: Naming the location, the source of the rules, a triggering description and a clear finish line gets you a skill that works the first time.

mission.title: Command Crafter
mission.intro: Kip keeps a toolbelt of tricks. Build your first custom command and skill in a real repo.
checklist: Type `/` in a session and browse the built-in command menu
Create `.claude/commands/standup.md` that summarizes recent git commits, using `$ARGUMENTS` for the time range
Run `/standup yesterday` and tweak the file until the output is useful
Create `.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` with a clear description, then ask a task that matches it
Run `/skills` to confirm your skill is listed
mission.explanation: Reusable commands and skills turn your best prompts into one-keystroke tools.

cheatsheet.description: Open the command menu; type letters to filter.
Start a new conversation with empty context.
Summarize the conversation to free up context.
Create a CLAUDE.md guide for the project.
Roll conversation and/or code back to an earlier point.
Replaced with everything typed after the command name.
Project skill: frontmatter plus instructions, loaded when relevant.
List skills available in this session.
Set true so only you can invoke the skill.
Autocomplete hint showing the expected arguments.
